Dear Mr. Henshaw, the epistolary novel by Beverly Cleary that won the Newbery Medal in 1984. Leigh Botts is a sixth-grader working through his parents' divorce by writing letters to his favorite author, Boyd Henshaw. He starts as a fan-boy seeking connection with his idol, but gradually transforms his correspondence into something deeper—a vehicle for processing his loneliness, his anger at adults, and his confusion about his absent father. The novel is structured entirely through Leigh's letters and diary entries, giving readers unfiltered access to his inner life without any authorial commentary between them. Mr. Henshaw's role is minimal but crucial. His kind, brief responses encourage Leigh to keep writing and to explore his own feelings, modeling how mentorship can be quiet and generative. What makes the book remarkable is how it captures the texture of childhood experience—the small humiliations, the conflicting loyalties, the slow growth of wisdom. Cleary treats the emotional reality of a grieving child with remarkable tenderness, and in doing so, she pioneered a work of children's literature that validates children's deepest feelings around loss and separation. More than that, the novel suggests that writing itself is transformative. Leigh becomes a writer not as a career path but as a way of surviving and understanding his world. He shares this epistolary journey with readers who themselves might find, in these pages, that words can be a lifeline.
